body: Policy vs political neutrality: ministers may lack specialised knowledge of policy and governance, so civil servants advise them on the right course. Political neutrality ≠ policy neutrality: an officer may prefer one policy over another while staying within legality and constitutionality. Involvement in policy = purely intellectual, never emotional. Civil servants must understand politics, not play politics, and must consider the political implications of policies they recommend.

Problems: a thinking person can never be completely neutral · the 4Cs of the political environment (criminalisation, casteism, communalism, corruption) make neutrality difficult · parties may demand loyalty instead of encouraging neutrality · no complete agreement on fundamentals such as the country's vision and direction (extreme right, extreme left, secular parties) · rise of multi-party democracy exposes officers to pressure from different parties at Centre and state.

body: Way forward: consistent political support with broad cross-party consensus · build capacity via targeted training, dedicated reform units, clear accountability frameworks · involve civil servants in design and delivery, with incentives incl. career advancement · safety nets (retraining, compensation, institutional support) · tailor reforms to states and regions · institutionalise regular consultation, transparent decisions, feedback. Aim: a more responsive, efficient, accountable bureaucracy.

Core shift: rules-based → roles-based HR (launched by GoI in 2020 as the National Programme for Civil Services Capacity Building; seen as one of the most comprehensive, institutionalised civil-service reforms since Independence; aim: dynamic, agile, citizen-centric bureaucracy). Aims: future-ready workforce · shift from rule-bound generalist administration to competency-driven, specialist governance · align with Viksit Bharat 2047 · performance-based appraisal over tenure-based promotion.

body: OECD: an environment where policy objectives, legal and institutional frameworks, decisions, their rationale and relevant information reach the public in a comprehensible, accessible, timely way.
UNESCAP: decisions and their enforcement follow rules and regulations; information is freely available and directly accessible to those affected by decisions.

In governance: people have the right to know what government is doing and government has an obligation to tell; criteria, processes and systems of decision-making are openly known to all (Tandon, 2002). Example: under Skill India Mission, citizens should know eligibility criteria, who applies them, benefits and conditions. TI: those affected should know the mechanisms and processes behind decisions, not just facts and figures. Open government: run openly so citizens can trust elected representatives and institutions. Public scrutiny: actions must withstand scrutiny, with information in an understandable form.

Objectives in detail: transparency makes govt accountable; raises chances of detecting corruption and deters it (TI Global Corruption Report 2003 stressed information); lets citizens access entitlements; improves service delivery; informed citizens understand decisions and reasons; participation in democracy needs access to information; lack of information breeds disempowerment, mistrust, frustration.

Transparency is the precursor of accountability, integrity and probity. Ethical governance needs not only rule of law but fairness, equality and justice. Mechanisms: RTI, e-governance, Citizens' Charters. Key measures: RTI 2005, NDSAP 2012, Charters, e-governance, CPGRAMS.

Social accountability stresses civic engagement: citizens help monitor govt performance. Tools: social audits (e.g. MGNREGA), public expenditure tracking, Citizen Report Cards, public hearings. They raise service quality and deter corruption by making governance participatory.

body: Responsibility = obligation to carry out assigned tasks at any level of the hierarchy. Accountability = responsibility operating hierarchically (the "hierarchical locus of responsibility"); simply, answerability for one's actions or behaviour. Public service accountability = how an agency or official fulfils duties and how they must account for it. Govt servants must work in the public interest and answer for what they do or fail to do. Needs acceptance of responsibility (others may evaluate performance) and openness (transparent working, ways to hold officers accountable).

Bureaucratic accountability has two aspects: Answerability = giving an account of actions taken or not taken; Enforceability = penalties or corrective measures for illegal, inadequate or improper performance.

notes: Financial/fiscal: one of the oldest; scrutiny of financial records so spending is authorised and lawful; legislature exercises its power over the public purse; may reveal corruption, kickbacks, misuse of welfare funds. World Bank says it needs: a working govt accounting system (expenditure control, cash management), an external audit system, and mechanisms to review audit findings and ensure corrective action
Process: how agencies do their tasks; detects procedural irregularities (improper tenders, contracts, construction procedures)

Programme: results and effectiveness; spending is not enough, objectives must be met (poverty programmes: were beneficiaries correctly identified? did living standards improve?); looks beyond efficiency to effective implementation
Legal: actions must comply with laws and judicial processes; court action and judicial review
Professional: doctors, engineers etc. follow professional codes while protecting the larger public interest
Political: concerns legitimacy of programmes; administrators must recognise the authority of elected representatives to set priorities, allocate resources, ensure compliance with lawful decisions
Social: citizens and civil society hold public institutions accountable, directly or indirectly (civic engagement)
Moral: core of public administration; goes beyond obeying laws and rules; a moral official strives for moral government; rising administrative and political corruption raises demand for it
World Bank: micro-accountability = govt responsiveness to citizens receiving services; macro = financial accountability and accountability for overall economic performance

body: Need for transparency and accountability: expanding govt role (growing, overlapping departments) · delegated legislation (more executive power) · politics-bureaucracy nexus (bureaucrats may become committed to a ruling party's agenda, not settled policy) · corruption (black money, opportunistic politics, scams) · limited popular participation (illiteracy, poverty, unemployment; benefits may not reach the needy; transparency lets citizens question misuse of money and power). How: several mechanisms together: traditional (ministerial control, debates, legislative committees, media, ombudsman) + New Public Management (efficiency, outcomes, competition, value for money, autonomy, partnerships, citizen orientation), which raise three questions: accountability for what (standards), to whom (agents), through what (means).

notes: CVC: set up Feb 1964 on Santhanam Committee advice; statutory status by CVC Act 2003; independent vigilance body; monitors vigilance in the Central govt; advises organisations on planning, executing, reviewing, reforming vigilance

notes: all citizens have the right

public authority: body or institution of self-government set up by/under the Constitution, by Parliament or state-legislature law, or by govt notification/order; includes bodies owned, controlled or substantially financed and NGOs substantially financed (directly or indirectly) by govt funds; "substantially" not defined in the Act (ARC made recommendations)

body: Public-interest override: despite the Official Secrets Act 1923 and the Sec 8(1) exemptions, access may be allowed if the disclosure outweighs the harm to protected interests. Only absolute exemption: copyright held by a person other than the State. Parliament test: what cannot be denied to Parliament cannot be denied to citizens. Second Schedule: Act does not apply to listed intelligence and security agencies, but info on allegations of corruption and human-rights violations must still be given (human-rights info only after the Information Commission's approval); investigating agencies were not listed, but CBI and NIA were added by executive order. Third-party info: notice and hearing first (10 days). Act prevails over the OSA 1923 and any other inconsistent law; no court can entertain a suit about an order under the Act except by appeal under the Act; wholly retrospective (covers info held before the Act too). Exempt info is released after 20 years, except Cabinet decisions, legislature-privilege matters, and info affecting sovereignty and integrity, security, strategic, scientific, economic interests, foreign relations or inciting an offence.

Rights of citizens: right to information · choose the medium of request · choose the language (English, Hindi or local language of the application) · help in writing the request · no reason or personal details beyond contact details · told immediately if the request is transferred to another authority · help in accessing records if disabled · all fees waived for BPL · all fees waived if the authority misses the time limit · reasons for rejection, appeal period, appellate authority details · complaint to CIC/SIC if: cannot submit to PIO/APIO, refused access, no response in time, unreasonable fee, incomplete, misleading or false info, or any matter on accessing records.

annual reports (to be laid before the legislature): 21 of 29 ICs did not submit for 2019-20; SICs of AP and Telangana have not published since 2017 and Odisha since 2015-16
waning interest: media, activists, civil society must keep generating awareness but interest is fading

body: Impact: besides transparency it became a grievance-redressal tool · exposed corruption, wasteful expenditure, scams, junkets, false narratives, recruitment results and marks · rural sections gained access, largely through NGO help · became a national movement aiding Right to Food, Right to Education movements · more successful for personally relevant information; falls short where controversial info of large public interest is involved.

notes: repeal the Official Secrets Act
replace oath of secrecy with oath of transparency
periodically review Second Schedule to stop list inflation; drop bodies not needed

classification norms are laid down by MHA and not public; Public Records Act 1993 mandates a 5-year review of top secret, secret, confidential files for declassification or downgrade, but procedure and norms are also not public, so govt discretion must be checked
selection of ICs: selection committee to include the CJI instead of the Union Cabinet Minister; at least half of IC members from non-civil-service background

access: 4 regional CIC offices; organisations with more than 1 PIO to name a nodal PIO; PIOs in the Central Secretariat at least Deputy Secretary or Director; payment by stamps or postal orders; single-window agency in each district to receive requests for all PIOs; suo motu disclosure in print, free for reference
records and funds: independent public records office (Centre and states) as technical repository; one-time 1% of all flagship programme funds for 5 years for RTI infrastructure and manuals
training for civil servants, not just PIOs; awareness campaigns through credible NGOs; CIC and SIC to issue ready reckoners
National Coordination Committee chaired by the CIC for an organic CIC-SIC link
"substantially financed" = receiving 50% of operating costs for 3 years or at least Rs 1 crore of govt funding; bring such bodies under RTI; steps to check frivolous complaints

body: As old as civilisation: Kautilya's Arthashastra lists many ways a civil servant can be corrupt and specific measures to contain it. Present everywhere, only in varying degree; almost no human activity is untouched; it has contributed to the decline of empires and to reforms in religion. TI definition: private abuse of public office. Elephant Test: corruption may be hard to define or describe, but when a civil servant does something unethical, society knows it: easier to point out than to define.

notes: Is a gift a bribe? consider the donor's intent, the recipient's expectation, timing, value, the country's legal framework, and social acceptability

Culture varies: old school ties (UK: used to leverage favours, culturally accepted); lobbying and networking (USA: regulated by law, legal, not seen as corrupt); Blat (Russia: Soviet-era system of favours and reciprocal favours, culturally accepted); Guanxi (China: a favour done must be returned)

Public bodies only, or private sector too? Many say both, but casting the net too wide dilutes focus and makes corruption unmanageable; counter-view: if government is incorruptible, private-sector corruption will fall naturally

head: Pair
Meaning
rows: every section of society unanimously feels the behaviour is corrupt and must not be tolerated
society recognises it as corrupt but tolerates it (common: speed money)
wide differences between sections of the population on whether the behaviour is corrupt
public servant who does not seek bribes but does not refuse one if offered
public servant who actively seeks opportunities to benefit through corrupt means
faced widely by the common man: must bribe an official just to get his due; the official extorts
official and bribe-giver collude for gain at the cost of public interest; both gain illegally
small corruption at street-level bureaucracy that the common man meets regularly (e.g. speed money)
crony capitalism: business houses practise state capture, influencing government to frame policies that illegally benefit them; at the highest levels

body: Corruption in the wider sense goes beyond giving and taking bribes; it includes any behaviour that harms public interest: lethargy in assigned duties · dereliction or negligence of duty · repeated carelessness · non-punctuality · subjective interpretation of public interest · favouritism and nepotism · communalism, casteism, lynching, regional bias.

notes: CORRUPTION: Social: divisions, unsafe lives; Economic: extra tax, low investment; Political: money power, unrest; Security: laundering, poor defence; International: aid cut, Magnitsky

head: Implication
Detail (handout)
rows: divides society vertically (rich or well-connected get their due, the poor do not) and horizontally (favouring one caste or class, neglecting others) · insecurity: people stop reporting crime and cooperating with police, boosting criminals' morale and criminalisation · endangers lives: building collapses, fires from substandard material, false certificates · erodes the social fabric: general distrust

aid reduced: in African countries aid went to dictators, warlords, corrupt officials, so donors changed stance, even for poor countries · lower investment: investors wary; Paulo Mauro: differential between less and more corrupt countries can be as high as 12% · acts as an additional tax on investment (bribes, extortion) · lower government revenue (officials collude or extort in collection) · diverts spending to non-priority sectors to ease corruption · lowers govt efficiency · distorts fair competition (collusion, crony capitalism) · brain drain and capital flight · hard to join international clubs (Eastern Europe vs EU) · environmental damage via collusion with officials

raises officials' power: in a fair system discretion is limited; in a corrupt one officials use it for gain · more money power · pork-barreling: a project shown as public interest but actually serving corporates, officials and politicians · citizens' despair raises appeal of extremist politicians (xenophobia, radical solutions, populism) · mass unrest (India Against Corruption) · radical tendencies: left extremism and North-East insurgency fed by corruption, poor development, a cycle of violence
security forces' corruption aids money laundering, drug and human trafficking, arms smuggling; defence procurement corruption hurts contract quality

Magnitsky Act 2012: Magnitsky, a Russian lawyer prosecuted for exposing corruption; US Congress passed an anti-corruption law in his name, souring ties with Russia · German car insurance (1990s): high-end cars stolen and smuggled to Central Europe with corrupt officials' help; premiums skyrocketed; diplomatic row

body: Revisionism: a school of thought with not many takers: some corruption in civil services is not bad. Hypothesis: civil servants are largely lethargic, less motivated, prone to red tape and poorly paid, so efficiency is low; corruption increases bureaucratic efficiency in public work.

head: Psycho-social factor
Meaning (handout)
rows: behaviour = attitudes/predispositions inside the person + the environment around
high corruption correlates with low self-worth; people turn to materialism to raise it; low self-esteem puts the locus of control outside, so worth depends on how society values them
society sees govt as highly corrupt; persistent labelling and shaming; even honest employees are seen through a corrupt lens, a disincentive to be honest
bureaucrats near retirement turn more corrupt to keep the benefits they enjoyed
most civil servants do not seek opportunities, only a few do; but when opportunities come they commit corruption; so reduce opportunities
European studies: areas with more Protestants less corrupt, since Protestantism was born as a reaction to corruption in the Catholic Church
long history of corruption (lower bureaucracy corrupt since ancient times, as in Kautilya) makes society tolerant
no popular sanction against corruption; honest people are victimised
excess spending on marriages, dowry provoke officials to corruption

notes: poor salary at upper levels is blamed, but raising pay alone may not dent corruption much
consumerism feeds low self-esteem and so corruption
licence-permit-quota raj → clearance raj: so many clearances and NOCs before starting a venture; red tape gives incentive to be corrupt
willingness and ability: big MNCs have the clout to bribe their way to favourable policy
business houses do not cooperate: if all refused to pay bribes corruption would fall sharply, but they try to outbid and outdo each other for government favours
excessive legal protection for public servants against prosecution for corruption
Art 311: reasonable opportunity before action, so it is very hard to dismiss corrupt servants; a source of excessive protection
PCA 1988, Sec 19: sanction of the appointing authority before prosecution

CrPC Sec 197 (as in the handout): permission of the appointing authority to prosecute for any offence other than corruption linked to official duty. Sec 19 and Sec 197 were meant to protect honest servants from spurious allegations but are misused to protect the corrupt
delay in prosecution (inadequate judicial process)
no effective whistleblower law to protect honest officials
inadequate autonomy of CBI and CVC, which have become politicised

flow.title: THE Sanction Chain
steps: DSPE Act 1946: preliminary inquiry first, then full investigation; prior sanction needed for investigation, not for preliminary inquiry. Single Directive: for Joint Secretary rank and above, sanction needed for both
Vineet Narain 1997: apex court struck the Single Directive down
DSPE Act amended: made law as Sec 6A
2014: SC struck down Sec 6A: violated equality (special protection to JS and above)
PCA amended 2018, Sec 17A: permission needed for preliminary inquiry into all public servants except those caught red-handed

notes: administrative: procedural complexity breeds middlemen who carry the corrupt money; red tape; weak internal grievance machinery; peer pressure and indoctrination make honest officials afraid to pursue anti-graft action; bureaucratic resistance to reform; politicised management through transfers and plum postings; general culture of secrecy

political: no political will (repeated attempts to pass the Lokpal Bill, delay in appointing Lokpal); criminalisation of politics (criminals inside the system protect themselves); system does not encourage neutrality: officials take sides when a dispensation is in power; lack of voter maturity (ousted parties re-elected; TINA: There Is No Alternative); money power in elections; weak disclosure norms on functioning and funding of parties

body: Official statistics: usable, but if prosecution and investigation are ineffective, they give an incomplete picture. Perceptual and attitudinal surveys: especially by international NGOs.

CPI by Transparency International · annual since 1995 · 0 = most corrupt, 100 = least corrupt. 2020 CPI (released 2021): New Zealand and Denmark least corrupt; Somalia, South Sudan last; South Asia: Bhutan 24th; USA 25th, Botswana 35th, China 78th, Pakistan 124th (as printed).

CPI critique: based on questionnaires to country experts and business leaders, not the common man · scores rest on perception, not objective assessment · sources change year to year · number of countries surveyed varies, so comparing ranks over years is inappropriate.

Other tools: Experiential surveys: TI's Global Corruption Barometer (actual experience; not annual, regional; in Asia, Japan least corrupt and India most corrupt among 17 countries) · Tracking surveys: World Bank PETS (tracks funds and flows at different levels when donor funds are spent) · content analysis of media (crude but interesting).

meta.title: THE Problem OF Corruption
meta.pyq: Mains 2016 · 2019 · 2014 · Handout M2 · Corruption
meta.simple: Corruption is misuse of public power for private gain. Learn the types, why it happens, what it costs and how it is measured, each with an example.
recall: accepts if offered vs actively seeks

body: Wicked problem: despite multiple laws (PCA, Lokpal, CVC Act) corruption persists; a proliferation of laws often signals systemic inefficiency. Corruption can only be controlled, not eliminated.

notes: TACKLING: Stick: prosecute, one agency; Carrot: pay, helplines; Admin: rotation, audit, e-gov; Radical: disband, amnesty; International: FCPA, UNCAC

Legal system and prosecution: higher conviction rates deter (e.g. Botswana); in India delayed trials and lenient punishment cut deterrence; harsh penalties like China's are unsuitable because of rule-of-law gaps and risk of victimisation

Stings and entrapment: admissibility of sting evidence is ambiguous; natural stings (citizen recordings) should be admissible; legal clarity needed to avoid misuse, as Sweden's restrictive stance shows
Tighten anti-corruption laws: 2018 amendments diluted the PCA; political will lacking to plug loopholes in whistleblower law, CVC Act, Lokpal Act
Declaration of assets: monitor disproportionate lifestyle indicators and run rigorous audits
Effective agencies: India's fragmented set (CVC, CBI, Lokpal, ED) lacks focus; Singapore (CPIB) and Hong Kong (ICAC) succeed with a single dedicated agency
Public shaming and blacklisting: naming corrupt officials (South Africa), blacklisting firms from public contracts: soft deterrents
Penalties on financial security: forfeiting pensions and future benefits creates fear of long-term loss
substantial pay increase, if paired with strict enforcement, can improve integrity at entry level
citizen-centric helplines: Delhi's anti-corruption hotline lets citizens report bribe demands without fear; replication needs effective whistleblower and witness protection laws
job rotation: frequent transfers in sensitive posts break entrenched networks (Kautilya supports)
auditing: CAG's limited coverage (25% of auditable units a year) hampers oversight; more manpower, IT tools, random audits
procurement: internal bid norms and a comprehensive Public Procurement Law; procurement is 30% of GDP and corruption-prone; 2012 bill lapsed, revival urgent
digitisation: online delivery cuts physical interface, curbing petty corruption
CCTV in high-risk zones (police stations, borders, vulnerable departments), high-risk first
Departmental disbanding (Georgia): non-reformable departments (Traffic Police, 2004) disbanded; fresh recruitment under stricter norms
Gender balance (Peru): more women in bureaucracy showed less corruption; could be piloted in India
Monetising bribes (Romania): allowing official payments to avoid petty bribes (as in its conscription policy); controversial on equity grounds
General amnesty: to disclose black money (with 50% surrender); debated; stricter enforcement essential after it

body: International: US FCPA 1977 and UK Bribery Act 2010 penalise MNCs' offshore corrupt practices · OECD Anti-Bribery Convention 1997 and UNCAC 2003 promote global norms · FATF 1989 fights money laundering · Interpol IGEC sets corruption standards for police · WTO's inaction on corruption as a non-tariff barrier is a missed chance · push for global financial transparency against banking havens. Critique: Western countries ignored corruption until the 1990s; post-globalisation it became a geopolitical tool; the "anti-corruption industry" with vested NGO interests often prioritises data production over ground impact; cultural imperialism concerns. Alternatives: spiritual education (ethics and meditation in curricula for internal integrity); Integrity Recognition Certificates (officially recognise honest officers to build peer-pressure networks; must be insulated from politicisation).

Definition: details of how a scheme is implemented and its resources, financial and non-financial, are shared with beneficiaries on a public platform (Jan Sunwai, public hearing, Gram Sabha); people can hold the local bureaucracy and Panchayat leaders accountable and judge the real impact. With local people involved, funds, resources, beneficiaries and records are laid bare; people spot loopholes, which checks corruption, raises transparency, fixes accountability and strengthens democracy. Unless public agencies must fully reveal scheme details, social audit is a lost cause: key = sound access to information.

notes: multi-perspective: helps beneficiaries and local leaders and civil servants, who can present their side when loopholes are found
regular: periodic, so issues are re-evaluated continuously
comparative: compares over time and across villages to show weaknesses and good practice
strengthens demand side: builds pressure on local bureaucracy to implement honestly; directly targets demand-side weaknesses, indirectly supply-side ones
more people's participation
benefits reach the targeted persons
social capital: community-building; people come together to bring change
identifies human-resource and training needs of civil servants
highlights development concerns
promotes transparency, checks corruption
helps frame better programmes later
not part of mainstream policy discourse
statutory in very few programmes (NREGA is one)
lack of trained social auditors
opposition from vested interests

symptom-cause relationship: fixing only surface symptoms (awareness drives for plague without tackling poor sanitation, congested housing) gives minimal impact; a scheme's failure at a remote symptom level should not justify dropping it unless all causal layers are examined; audits must assess multiple cause-effect layers, so trained auditors are essential

Legal and institutional: model national social audit law inspired by Meghalaya's 2017 Act for all public service schemes (community ownership, accountability); independent audit units: autonomous, well-resourced, professionally staffed (AP SSAAT); strengthen CAG oversight and build PRIs' technical and human-resource capacity

Stakeholders: grassroots campaigns for Gram Sabha members; structured auditor training in standards and ethics; partner NGOs and media to amplify findings; recognition for active Gram Sabha participants

Standardise and digitise: online portals with real-time audit reports, scheme spending, PRI records; proactive disclosure of project data; unified audit guidelines and checklists for uniformity and comparability

Best practices: Chhattisgarh: link audits with grievance redressal; wall writing for community transparency; Karnataka: rotate audit teams after every 3 audit cycles to prevent familiarity and collusion

head: Success story
Detail
rows: autonomous Society for Social Audit, Accountability and Transparency; trained village-level resource persons; crores misappropriated in wages recovered; World Bank lauded it as a global best practice in participatory accountability
independent audits exposed ghost beneficiaries, wage delays, PDS ration diversion; SC in Swaraj Abhiyan (2016) appreciated social audits; built local capacity, empowered Gram Sabhas
jan sunwais in the 1990s revealed massive leakages; movement led to RTI Act 2005
a civil society organisation pioneered CRCs; surveys on water supply, public hospitals, transport; bribery fell, satisfaction rose; endorsed in a 2003 study; globally recognised
local bodies compared service delivery costs (e.g. cost per km of road); public disclosure built citizen pressure on inefficient bodies, cutting urban corruption

notes.ca: In the news · Saarthi IAS CA, Jul/Aug 2026 (verify)Low Gram Sabha participation (NIRDPR study): barriers: livelihood and time (55.5%), exclusion of migrants, women, youth, elderly; trust fatigue. Impact: elite capture; social audits become a formality; Niyamgiri 2013 (12 Gram Sabhas rejected mining). Way: Action Taken Reports; off-peak meetings; Kudumbashree; ARC-II statutory powers.

DSPE Act 1946 sets up CBI for anti-corruption investigation; RPA 1951 Sec 123: corrupt practices in elections; PCA 1988: general anti-corruption law; Benami Properties Act 1988; PMLA 2003: nodal law on money laundering; CVC Act; RTI 2005 (transparency, accountability); state Lokayuktas Acts; Lokpal Act 2013; Whistleblower Act 2014; time-bound service delivery laws (to tackle speed money)
Institutions: CBI, CVC, state anti-corruption bureaus and vigilance wings, CAG, Lokayuktas, Lokpal, ED (principally PMLA and FEMA), Banking Sector Ombudsman, Consumer Courts, the 3-tier judiciary

steps: Special Police Establishment, 1941
DSPE Act 1946: statutory backing
Popular name CBI, 1963

head: CBI division
Handles
rows: economic offences in banking and securities markets

notes: politicisation: a former SC judge called CBI a "caged parrot"; every ruling party at the Centre has used such bodies against political opponents, so it is not impartial or autonomous
staff shortage: about one-third of posts vacant
conviction rate 67% is high vs 30-40% for other agencies, but low in high-profile cases

sanction for prosecution: long delays in disposal (partly staff shortage); after investigation comes prosecution, but PCA Sec 19 and CrPC Sec 197 give civil servants undue protection and sanction must come from the government (state govt, per handout); delay in sanction means delay in prosecution
no suo motu jurisdiction: CBI handles only cases transferred to it

body: Single Directive struck down · CVC superintends CBI on PCA cases · Appointment of Director by a committee · Tenure minimum 2 years · Transfer by the same committee · Executive (DoPT) sets only the policy framework · Reproach remains: still called a "caged parrot". (own mnemonic)

notes: CVC supervises CBI: CVC deals largely with anti-corruption cases and civil-service discipline violations; the CVC Act gives it general superintendence over CBI in PCA cases
minimum guaranteed tenure for the Director and other key CBI posts; under the DSPE Act, 2 years for the Director; an ordinance allows extension up to 5 years, after the 2 years, in tranches of 1 year

Director's appointment not left to the govt's sole discretion: committee of the PM, Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha (or leader of the largest opposition party if there is no recognised LoP) and the CJI; the transfer of the Director also needs the same committee
Single Directive struck down
DoPT: CBI is under its broad direction and control, but only for the overall policy framework, not day-to-day work or investigations

flow.title: CVC Timeline
steps: 1962 Santhanam Committee
1964 executive body
2003 CVC Act: statutory

body: 1 Commissioner + up to 2 Vigilance Commissioners · term 4 years · age 65 · no reappointment.

notes: chosen from two categories: persons who are or were in All India or Central Services, and officers of CPSUs; selecting from both ensures at least one from each
committee: PM, Home Minister, Leader of Opposition (or leader of the largest opposition party); the govt effectively has the final say through its two representatives

P.J. Thomas case 2011: SC held that the govt's majority made the LoP's membership pointless, so selection must rest on consensus, not majority (the ruling applied to this appointment, not all committee appointments)
term: 4 years, retirement age 65; no reappointment to the same post, but a Vigilance Commissioner can be elevated to CVC if total stay stays within 4 years
pay and conditions: CVC = UPSC Chairperson; VCs = UPSC members; cannot be altered to their disadvantage; paid from the Consolidated Fund of India
barred from appointment as UT administrator, diplomatic assignments or any post made under the President's warrant and seal; no office of profit under Centre or states

removal: proven misbehaviour or incapacity through a reference to the Supreme Court; other grounds: insolvency, moral turpitude, private employment, infirmity of body and mind, prejudicial financial interests
superintend and give directions to CBI in PCA 1988 corruption cases (as directed in Vineet Narain)
inquire or cause inquiry on a Central Government reference, or on complaints against Group A officials, AIS officers and equivalent CPSU officials (Sec 8(2) CVC Act 2003)
review progress of DSPE investigations under PCA and of pending applications for sanction of prosecution
advice to Central Govt and organisations on referred matters; superintendence over vigilance administrations of ministries and organisations; civil-court powers in inquiries
mandatory consultation before the Centre makes rules on vigilance or disciplinary matters of Union services and AIS members

CVC is chair (Vigilance Commissioners members) of the committee recommending the Director of Enforcement (and ED officers at Deputy Director level and above, after consulting the Director) and of the committee recommending CBI officers of SP rank and above except the Director, incl. extension or curtailment of their tenure
annual report to the President, who places it before Parliament

body: Issues: overwhelming dependence on CBI for investigation, and CBI is politicised and government-controlled · no independent prosecution power; sanction needs government permission, often delayed · cases of non-cooperative attitude of government · poor engagement with civil society, citizens, NGOs in the same field.

Suggestions (handout, with examples): give CVC independent investigative and prosecution powers like Lokpal (2nd ARC Ethics report: functional autonomy for vigilance agencies, less reliance on politicised CBI) · statutory 3-6 month timelines for prosecution sanction (Vineet Narain fixed timelines, but TI India 2023: over 70% pending beyond 6 months) · make CVC advice a binding oversight over vigilance in ministries and PSUs (Sarkaria) · more manpower and technology: dedicated vigilance cadre, digital monitoring (CVC annual report 2023: under 50% of sanctioned staff, over 1500 organisations) · civil society participation, public grievance dashboard (2nd ARC; South Korea's ACRC) · binding recommendations via amending CVC Act (Punchhi Commission) · transparent selection: add judiciary members or eminent anti-corruption experts (P.J. Thomas 2011).
Flag: CVC Selection Committee (PM, HM, LoP) differs from Lokpal (PM, Speaker, LoP, CJI, jurist).

meta.title: CBI & CVC
meta.pyq: Mains 2021* · Handout M2 · Institutions
meta.simple: CBI investigates, CVC watches. Vineet Narain (1997) put the CVC over the CBI and gave the Director a fixed tenure.

timeline: Sweden ombudsman
UK Parliamentary Commissioner
India's first Lokpal Bill introduced
Maharashtra Lokayukta
Bill passed = Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act
Lokpal constituted: Justice P.C. Ghose

body: Lokpal = ombudsman or watchdog of administration; first came into existence in Sweden, 1809. UK: designated Parliamentary Commissioner, set up 1967. USA: ombudsman only in some states (Hawaii, Oregon, Nebraska), not federal. First ARC: two-tier set-up: Lokpal to probe officials of Secretary rank and above at Union and State levels; a Union Lokayukta for officials below Secretary rank at the Union level; State Lokayuktas for similar cases in states. India: first Bill introduced 1968; present Bill passed 2013 (became the Act); Lokpal constituted 2019, Justice P.C. Ghose Chairperson of the nine-member body. Maharashtra first state to appoint a Lokayukta (1971).

notes: flooded with complaints: an apex body's efficiency depends on lower departments handling petty complaints well
poor effectiveness: powers inadequate to investigate and prosecute properly
inter-state differences in qualifications, tenure, functions, powers, suo motu powers; no separate investigation agency
survival at the state government's sweet will: created and abolished by states; Odisha abolished it by ordinance in 1992; Haryana, 1999
paper tigers: mostly recommendatory
corruption within Lokayuktas (allegations of extortion)
misused to intimidate political opponents

body: 9 members · 25 years' experience · min age 45 · term 5 years or 70.

notes: nine-member body including the Chairperson
Chairperson: is or has been a CJI or SC judge, or an eminent person with 25 years' experience in vigilance, anti-corruption, law, finance, administration, management
8 members: half judicial (SC judge or High Court Chief Justice), half non-judicial (eminent person with 25 years' experience in the same fields)
50% affirmative action: opportunity for SC, ST, OBC, minorities, women
not an MP, MLA or MLC; not a member of any local body
minimum age 45
not removed or dismissed from government service
no other office of profit, no business activity or profession
no affiliation with any political party

flow.title: Appointment
steps: Selection committee may appoint a 7-member search committee to shortlist (also with 50% affirmative action) but may go beyond its names
Selection committee: PM (Chair), Speaker, LoP in Lok Sabha, CJI or SC judge nominated by him, eminent jurist chosen by those four
Appointed under the name and seal of the President on its recommendation
Tenure 5 years or age 70; no reappointment, except a member elevated to Chairperson within a total of 5 years

body: Gap: the Act does not say who replaces the Leader of Opposition if there is no recognised LoP in Lok Sabha.

Pay: Chairperson = CJI; member = SC judge; terms cannot be altered to their disadvantage in office. Disabilities after retirement: like CVC, plus cannot contest any election in India for 5 years. Wings: Inquiry wing (Director of Inquiry), Prosecution wing (Director of Prosecution), Secretary of Lokpal, appointed from a panel recommended by the Government of India.
2nd ARC opposed covering the PM: it would cripple administration while an investigation runs · foreign powers may exploit it to malign the PM · the PM is already covered by the PCA 1988.

Arguments for covering the PM: CBI works under DoPT, i.e. the PM's direct control, which would hamper investigation · the PM should lead by example; some states' Lokayuktas already cover the CM · Art 361 exempts only the President and Governors; no legal or constitutional exemption for the PM.

notes: PM (partially), Union Ministers, MPs, Group A-D officials, and functionaries of boards, corporations, societies, trusts funded by govt (receiving above Rs 10 lakh a year)
any individual may complain for offences under the PCA 1988

flow.title: FLOW OF A Complaint
steps: Complaint → Lokpal may order a preliminary inquiry by its Inquiry Wing, CVC or agencies like CBI; first seeks the public servant's explanation to find a prima facie case; Group C and D complaints go to the CVC; inquiry ends in 60 days

After the inquiry report and a hearing of the public servant, Lokpal can: order full investigation, start departmental proceedings, close the case, or proceed against the complainant if allegations are false
Investigating agencies report to Lokpal and the court; a Lokpal Bench (min 3 members) decides on sanction to prosecute, departmental action, or closure
Lokpal replaces the appointing/dismissing authority in granting prosecution sanction under CrPC 218 and PCA 19

body: Powers: search, seizure, asset attachment, Civil Procedure Code powers for inquiries, superintendence over CBI for cases Lokpal refers. Removal: on grounds of misbehaviour, through a reference to the Supreme Court, but only if signed by at least 100 MPs; on other grounds (insolvency, private employment, infirmity of body or mind, prejudicial financial interest) the President may dismiss on the advice of the Council of Ministers. Also: annual declaration of assets and liabilities by public servants · annual report to the President, tabled in Parliament, with a memorandum explaining why recommendations were rejected · 7-year limitation period for filing complaints.

notes: jurisdiction too wide
very convoluted appointment process
PM only partially covered
7-year limitation period is a limit
wide scope can lead to intimidation of NGOs
delays in appointments

Functioning since 2019: allegations of emasculating the body through legislation; govt delayed rules on the complaint form, asset disclosure, and Lokpal's rules for preliminary inquiry and investigation; prosecution and investigation wings not set up by 2020; yet by Sept 2019 it had disposed of 1,000 of 1,065 complaints; complaints keep falling: 1,427 (2019-20) → 110 (2020-21) → 12 till August of 2021-22
give constitutional status (now only statutory) to both the Union and State bodies, for independence and respect
Rashtriya Lok Ayukta (Union level): Union Ministers, MPs, State Chief Ministers
State Lokayukta: State Ministers and state legislatures
CVC should handle civil servants
Local Bodies Ombudsman for political and administrative officials of local bodies

body: Not a panacea: corruption is a hydra-headed monster, needing a multi-pronged strategy · the bureaucracy is huge, so Lokpal cannot handle all complaints · how well govt bodies deal with petty complaints should be examined, since Lokpal gets them too · inadequate judicial process · developed nations have an ombudsman, empowered citizens and willingness to complain; India lacks these.

meta.title: Lokpal IN India
meta.pyq: Mains 2013 · Handout M2 · Lokpal
meta.simple: The Lokpal is the ombudsman for central corruption cases. The Act is detailed, but the body has been slow and thinly used.
recall: First Bill introduced; Bill passed (Act); Lokpal constituted

body: PIDPI Act 2014 (Public Interest Disclosure and Protection of Individuals making Disclosure): anyone can be a whistleblower about any public body or agency. Disclosure goes to the competent authority. No anonymous complaints. The CVC can issue directions for protection. Frivolous complaints: 2 years' jail. A 2015 amendment bill (introduced, later lapsed) proposed that the Official Secrets Act 1923 should override the Whistleblowers Act. (Handout also describes it as a mechanism to receive complaints on corruption or wilful misuse of power or discretion, with inquiry and safeguards against victimisation.)

notes: lack of anonymity: the Act mandates disclosing the whistleblower's identity, exposing them to retaliation; the murder of Satyendra Dubey, who reported corruption in the NHAI, shows the danger and discourages whistleblowers
weak organisational implementation: no clear guidelines or awareness, so employees hesitate to use official channels

body: Digital divide: 75% of net users are in urban India; digital illiteracy in rural India (an illiterate person cannot use online services even with a smartphone); mirrors the urban-rural divide (COVID: urban middle-class students on Zoom, rural students excluded; imbalance in education); rural people miss income opportunities, telemedicine; elderly more vulnerable; inadequate vernacular content; last-mile connectivity still a problem.
Digital trust: entering personal information for transactions or fee payment makes people insecure about misuse of data.

Teacher's 6 C's of work plan: Content development (revise regularly, relevant to the zone) · Competence building (e.g. bank staff blame "server fault" and wait for an expert: give basic ICT training) · Connectivity, esp. rural (else only the integrated part benefits, majority left on margins) · Citizen's interface (needs phone and internet; internet costly for rural people; awareness; accessible and affordable) · Cyber laws (data protection and security; technology-agnostic; balance privacy so that productive use of technology is not compromised) · Capital (sites need revenue streams; reasonable charges, self-sustaining).

Inadequate re-engineering: e-governance lets government restructure and simplify procedure; if not done, procedure never gets digitised. Delay is not because of support agencies but sometimes govt lacks interest in simplifying, as the corruption point barricades digitisation.

Narrow vision, no consultation: services shifted from physical to digital without asking stakeholders whether it fits their needs; if consulted first and physical-world problems resolved, e-governance matches needs. Check on corruption and transparency only incidental: dip is automatic from removing human interface; design intervention for the twin goals of accountability and transparency.

notes: preamble: right to privacy is a fundamental right; protect personal data as a facet of privacy; collective culture for a free and fair digital economy
applies to: government, companies incorporated in India, foreign companies dealing with personal data of individuals in India

personal data: traits or attributes of identity that identify an individual; sensitive: financial, biometric, caste, religious or political belief, or other category the government specifies with the Authority and sectoral regulator

data fiduciary: entity or individual deciding means and purpose of processing; only for specific, clear, lawful purposes, within collection and storage limits; security safeguards (encryption, preventing misuse), grievance redress, age verification and parental consent for sensitive data of children

rights of data principal: confirmation of processing, correction of inaccurate/incomplete/out-of-date data, portability to another fiduciary, restrict continuing disclosure when no longer necessary or consent withdrawn
consent is the basis; no consent needed for: benefits by the State, legal proceedings, medical emergency

Authority: protects individuals' interests, prevents misuse, ensures compliance; chair + 6 members with at least 10 years in data protection and IT; appeal to Appellate Tribunal, then Supreme Court
transfer abroad: sensitive data only with explicit consent plus conditions, and must still be stored in India; critical personal data (notified) processed only in India

exemptions: Centre can exempt its agencies (security of state, public order, sovereignty and integrity, friendly relations, preventing incitement to cognizable offences); also prevention/investigation/prosecution of offences, personal or domestic, journalistic purposes (still specific, clear, lawful, with safeguards)

body: Governance has two aspects: process/institutions (state, market, NGOs, legal frameworks) and substantive content (how it addresses health, education etc.). In a welfare state like India the state is the principal problem-solving forum and its legitimacy lay in its capacity to address public issues, defining India's model until the 1991 reforms. Over time structural inefficiencies showed it could not tackle complex challenges single-handedly; post-1990s reforms shifted to market delivery; three decades on the market's exploitative tendencies and limits are evident: so civil society emerged as the third forum (inclusivity, transparency, participatory decisions).

body: Civil society = people organising themselves outside state and market (NGOs may get donations from state or market but are created by people and largely outside them): an intermediate space; the "fifth estate" (after legislature, executive, judiciary and media). Voluntary (organised on the principle of voluntarism) · collective interest · autonomous · largely self-supporting · bound by shared values · citizens acting collectively in the public sphere · does not seek formal power. Political parties and media are kept out. No universally accepted definition: a mafia satisfies all the characteristics yet is not civil society. It is not society in general but organised social life: people organising around common beliefs, values, interests (NGOs, interest, advocacy, philanthropic, social-activism groups).

Non-State, not anti-State: they operate outside the government machinery, which does not make them anti-State. Criticism is not opposition: in a functioning democracy dissent and watchdog activity strengthen the State by improving accountability. Treating all civil society as suspect weakens democracy: blanket suspicion silences the legitimately voiceless alongside the genuinely problematic actor.

The concern is not baseless, only overextended: a small number may misuse funds or work against public interest, so proportionate, transparent regulation, the kind the 2nd ARC envisaged for FCRA, is legitimate. The failure is using that concern to justify blanket restriction.

Way forward: treat non-state actors as governance partners, not adversaries (service delivery, advocacy, innovation) · reform FCRA toward proportionality, decentralising administration as 2nd ARC suggested, distinguishing genuine financial misconduct from politically inconvenient advocacy · deepen SHG 2.0, addressing rising NPAs and credit weaknesses so SHGs evolve from a subsistence tool into economic empowerment infrastructure · modernise cooperative governance (PACS computerisation, Model Cooperative Societies Act, Ministry of Cooperation) · formal consultative mechanisms for pressure groups, not street mobilisation and informal lobbying alone · calibrate regulation to risk: target genuine wrongdoing without a chilling effect on legitimate civic work.

Social capital = power of the collective. Two pillars: trust and reciprocity. vs financial capital: both are productive; social capital is everywhere whereas financial capital is confined to financial institutions; social capital is unlimited and infinite, financial is finite.

body: SHG: principally a rural women's movement (not only women-specific; some include men); small, informal associations, not legally registered, not legal entities; largely poor women, preferably of similar socio-economic background; ideal size 10-20. Each must save regularly (weekly); a weekly loan corpus is created and lent to members for income-generating ventures, vulnerabilities, productive needs. A savings-led microfinance model to improve earnings and savings and build an economic base to escape poverty, on self-help and collective responsibility: loans carry no security (poor rural women lack the collateral financial institutions demand); repaid because of collective responsibility and peer pressure.

Bank link: when an SHG matures it is linked to a bank: it deposits its collective corpus, earns interest, and can avail a larger loan. Banks normally follow a 1:4 deposit-to-credit ratio (SHG depositing Rs 10,000 a month as corpus is eligible for four times that as loan).

body: Pressure group: hard to define (parties are sometimes included, sometimes excluded); the common definition excludes political parties and covers groups wishing to influence government policies and activities while remaining apart from government. An association of people with common interests who try to achieve them by influencing government; helps social integration, political articulation and acts as a catalyst for change. Definition: "an organised aggregate which seeks to influence the context of governmental decisions without attempting to place its members in formal governmental capacities". Alan R. Ball: firmly part of the political process; reinforce or change the direction of policy but do not wish to become the government. Henry Turner: non-partisan; do not draft party programmes or nominate candidates. Finer: "anonymous empire". R.D. Lambert: "unofficial government". Truman (group theory): a group, on the basis of shared attitudes (the interest), makes claims on other groups for the establishment, maintenance or enhancement of behaviour implied in those attitudes.

safety valve for grievances, preventing spontaneous outbursts
consensus building to present a united face to government (FICCI; Samyukt Kisan Morcha)
TECHNIQUES: Lobbying (CII, FICCI); PILs (CSE); Media, digital drives; Mass protests; Report cards, social audit; Research, coalitions; Satyagraha, fasts; RTI exposés (MPLADS)
lobbying and direct negotiation with policymakers, bureaucrats, legislators (CII, FICCI on tax reforms and industrial policy)
PILs for judicial intervention (CSE for air-pollution control)
media campaigns and opinion building (RTI activists exposing administrative opacity)
mass mobilisation: rallies, dharnas, petitions, signature drives (farmers' protests 2020-21)
social audits and citizen report cards (PAC report card reduced bribery in service delivery in Bangalore)
expert inputs and research-based advocacy: white papers, data to committees and ministries (PRS Legislative Research)
coalition building (NCPRI united civil society for the RTI Act)
strategic legal interventions: court cases, stay orders, amicus curiae
symbolic protests: satyagraha, padayatras, hunger strikes (Anna Hazare's Lokpal movement)
digital campaigns: hashtags, viral videos, petitions (#SaveAarey mobilised urban youth)
RTI-based exposes (MPLADS fund misuse)

body: Best practices: PAC report card (Bangalore: citizen audits cut corruption in municipal services) · NCPRI RTI campaign (coalition success, led to the RTI Act) · #SaveAarey (Mumbai, 2019: digital activism led to policy reversal on urban deforestation) · CEHAT (research-based lobbying shaped national policy on patient rights) · Anna Hazare's Jan Lokpal movement (2011: Gandhian methods put anti-corruption on the national agenda).

Lobbying: so called as big business leaders roamed the lobbies of the US Congress to influence policy. Today: formally connecting with government, regular meetings with officials and ministers, presenting the interests of the section one represents to get a favourable policy outcome; used principally by organised corporate groups, business houses, business associations. Not bad per se; in India neither legal nor illegal. Problems: (a) paid lobbyists: Nira Radia and Vaishnavi Corporate Communications (getting specific leaders placed in specific ministries); Deepak Talwar Associates (accused of bribing civil servants); (b) legislators as lobbyists: H.G. Mudgal disqualified from the provisional Parliament after Independence for lobbying for a private organisation (Bombay Bullion Organisation); (c) bureaucrats, serving or retired: advising the Minister to tweak rules for certain organisations, pushing files to accommodate a private player. Santhanam Committee 1962: proper system of accreditation of lobbyists; no civil servant should interact with a representative of a business organisation or group unless fully accredited.

Business associations (FICCI, ASSOCHAM, CII) methods: lobbying · political donations via electoral bonds · critical assessment of government economic policies/legislation · commissioning studies · workshops and conferences · technical inputs · appointment to advisory/ad hoc panels · consensus building · interaction with analogous institutions abroad, like WTO.

notes: disproportionate influence of some: caste and community groups, trade and peasant unions, business associations like FICCI, CII after 1991
subversion of democratic institutions: legislators and parties heavily influenced lose independent thinking
unorganised interests neglected (e.g. educational development)
extra-legal methods: bandhs, hartals, rail roko, chakka jam, destruction of public property
divisive: prevent emergence of a true national identity
block progressive initiatives: some Khap Panchayats sanction honour killings in inter-caste marriages
many lack transparency in internal functioning (e.g. RSS)

body: Khap Panchayats: SC 2011: a Khap advocating or sanctioning honour killing should be banned altogether under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act; an officer who does not check its illegal decisions would also be penalised. As victims are generally SC/ST, the accused can also be prosecuted under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989. Some states like Rajasthan proposed laws against honour killing, but regular IPC provisions (e.g. Sec 302) suffice if rationally enforced. Khaps thrive on weak local bodies, judicial inadequacies, political patronage. But some Khaps have done consensus building and socially oriented community service.

Effectiveness depends on: sectional (RSS, Khap Panchayats, caste associations: more effective in India) vs promotional (human rights organisations, PETA) · funding (lobbying needs a lot of money) · political branding (linked to certain parties, so effectiveness depends on that party's role in government) · membership (quantity and quality) · government reliance on them (Make in India needs business associations).

Way forward: legal recognition and regulatory framework: absence of formal status limits legitimacy and accountability; registration and regulation akin to US and UK lobbying laws · code of conduct and financial transparency: mandatory ethics, disclose funding sources and lobbying (vital in telecom, pharma where opaque lobbying undermines trust) · consultative role in legislative committees and policy dialogues (e.g. farmers' associations in agricultural reforms and MSP) · digital platforms like MyGov to gather feedback systematically.

body: Ambedkar in the Constituent Assembly: "the most important office under the Constitution"; one of the 4 pillars with SC, UPSC and Election Commission. Art 148 creates the office. Principal responsibility: audit accounts of State and Central governments spending taxpayers' money; so significant for financial accountability that it must have independence like the judiciary. Status: service conditions broadly equivalent to a Supreme Court judge, including salary and removal safeguards.

head: Point
Fact
rows: 6 years or until age 65, whichever is earlier, under the CAG (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971; changes require amending the Act, not the Constitution
Art 148(4): CAG ineligible for further government office under the Union or any State
prescribed under Art 149; laid down in the CAG (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, enacted by Parliament

notes: all expenditure from Consolidated Fund, Public Account, Contingency Fund of India / States / UTs with legislative assembly
trading, manufacturing accounts and profit and loss statements kept by any department of Centre, States, UTs with legislature (e.g. Railways, Posts)
receipts of Union and States: rules designed to secure an effective check on assessment and collection of revenue
stocks and stores and government inventory: ensure no pilferage
receipts and expenditure of bodies substantially financed by government; and of bodies not substantially financed when requested by the President or Governor
Public Sector Undertakings
advises the President on the form of accounts of Union and States (Art 150); certifies net proceeds shared by Union with States (Art 279)
assists the Finance Commission in a fair understanding of states' actual financial position
audits accounts of Autonomous District Councils under Schedule VI

body: Audit-on: Consolidated and other funds · Accounts (trading, P&L) · Receipts · Stores · Entities financed (bodies, PSUs). (own mnemonic)

head: PSU type
CAG audit
rows: Statutory corporations (special law, governed by own statute, generally government-owned; LIC, FCI, RBI)
CAG may conduct full, partial or no audit, depending on the law
Government companies (registered under Companies Act / joint stock; at least 51% government ownership)
audited by private auditors appointed in consultation with CAG; CAG can also do a supplementary audit over and above it

body: PSUs = government-owned enterprises for commercial and economic activity outside the regular departmental structure; some set up as State monopolies in strategic sectors. Performance audit: both categories may face comprehensive performance audit through the Audit Board (introduced 1968), where applicable.

Separation of accounting and auditing: accounts are prepared by the department or undertaking; audit is by an external authority for independence and no conflict of interest. Departmentalisation of Accounts (1976): before 1976 CAG did both compilation of accounts and audit; the scheme transferred preparation and compilation of Union accounts to ministries and departments, leading to the Indian Civil Accounts Service (ICAS) and the Controller General of Accounts (CGA) under the Finance Ministry. Now: CAG primarily audits Union accounts, continuing both accounting and auditing for most States, subject to arrangements. Significance: clearer separation, stronger financial accountability and independent oversight.

notes: no role of a broad-based committee as in NHRC, CVC, Information Commissioners; entirely at the discretion of the central government
UK: CAG heading the National Audit Office appointed by House of Commons resolution after agreement between PM and chair of PAC (generally an opposition member)
USA: Comptroller General heading GAO appointed by the President, ratified by the Senate
Australia: ratification and confirmation by the whole Public Accounts Committee

India is a member of ASOSAI and INTOSAI and should abide by their mission statement and charter so that complete independence is guaranteed; experts recommend a broad-based committee of PM, LoP in Lok Sabha and CJI for appointments like CAG, UPSC, Election Commission
experts: career auditors and accountants of the Indian Audit and Accounts Service (IAAS)
till date among 14 CAGs only the first three came from IAAS; of the remaining 11, 10 were retired IAS officers
adverse effect on morale and motivation of IAAS officers
conflict of interest: an IAS officer who served a department is asked to audit the same department as CAG
post-retirement incentive for IAS officers may lead to politicisation of civil services
so: encadre the post, earmarked only for IAAS members
Narhari Rao first CAG; K. Sanjay Murthy present (as per handout, verify)

body: Single vs multi-member body: experts debate making CAG multi-member like UPSC and Election Commission. But the real problem is understaffed IAAS, not single-member form: of about 250,000 auditable entities CAG effectively audits only about 60,000 a year, so more IAAS officers, ground staff and junior officers are needed. In the USA and UK too the CAG is a single-member body, with a heavier caseload than India's; no study shows a multi-member institution performs better.

head: Audit
Question it asks
rows: was money spent according to the financial law of the country? legal availability of money spent; was the mandated activity authorised by Parliament?
are proper books of accounts maintained; are recorded transactions a faithful representation of what actually took place?

e.g. number of schools set up under an amount, and their standards and facilities: efficiency of money spent. CAG does only performance audit/reporting, not performance evaluation; reasons for inefficiency are outside CAG's domain

questions the wisdom and faithfulness of government spending; e.g. 2G spectrum on first-come-first-served, audited by then CAG Vinod Rai: Rs 1.76 lakh crore revenue loss. Need: it is taxpayers' money, not officials' own, so officials cannot be expected to show the caution they would with their own; major frauds and scams come to light only through propriety audit

body: Four audits: Compliance · Financial · Performance · Propriety. The 1971 Act does not clearly state the types of audit; Sec 23 authorises CAG to define the scope of audit. (own mnemonic)

Against propriety audit: benefit of hindsight: a decision may look unwise without the context in which it was made · auditors know little of administration: seasoned auditors lack experience of decisions under administrative circumstances · red tapism: fear of CAG, CVC, CBI makes officials keep files undecided · slows development. Paul Appleby (1950s, American public-administration expert): CAG oversight created fear among civil servants and delayed decisions; he even recommended abolishing the office.

For: CAG's role is more than tallying accounts, "which any B.Com. graduate can do" · supreme audit institutions worldwide do propriety audit · CAG should not be nit-picking, but if a prima facie case of fraud, impropriety, irregularity comes up, exposing it is not just his right but his duty · purpose is not fault-finding but better financial governance · instead of questioning it, streamline internal audits and respond proactively to audit queries · best potential to expose irregularities, embezzlement, bribery, fraud.

2G case: 2008 licences allocated on First-Come-First-Served instead of auctions; CAG estimated a presumptive loss of up to Rs 1.76 lakh crore; government defended low spectrum prices as promoting affordable telecom; SC 2012 quashed 122 licences and directed fresh allocation by auction; the auction raised about Rs 9,400 crore, below expectations, partly due to changing market conditions and limited bidders. CAG's jurisdiction: normally examines policy implementation, but may question policy decisions where they involve financial irregularities, wasteful expenditure or loss to the exchequer (PYQ 2016)

notes.h: Comptroller vs Auditor; PPPs; Local Bodies

body: Comptroller function: before public money is released, verify that the expenditure has been authorised by Parliament and approve release of funds. Key difference: UK CAG exercises pre-expenditure control; Indian CAG audits after the money has been spent.

notes: PPP: government-private collaboration for infrastructure (highways, airports, ports); government gives approvals, land, support as agreed; private gives investment and expertise, develops and operates
BOT: private builds and operates for a concession period, recovers investment through tolls or user fees, then transfers to government

VGF: one-time or deferred government grant for economically justified but financially unviable PPP projects; 2020 VGF Scheme extended to social infrastructure (health, education, water supply, waste management)

question: PPPs may be largely privately financed, so what is CAG's jurisdiction? Public interest: public assets, natural resources, concessions, revenue sharing; irregularities in concession period, toll collection, revenue sharing harm public interest; so PPPs may fall in CAG purview, depending on applicable law and contract, even with private financing

Telecom revenue sharing: operators pay licence fees as a percentage of Adjusted Gross Revenue (AGR); underreporting or inadmissible deductions cut the government's share; AUSPI v Union of India (2014): SC upheld CAG's authority to examine private telecom operators' accounts to verify revenue-sharing payments

body: Local bodies (ULBs, PRIs): in some states CAG provides broad supervision and guidelines for local-body accounts and audit; it does not conduct audits as such; the broad overview is accepted by state governments principally to get the conditional grants recommended by the Finance Commission.

notes.h: WHY CAG IS WEAK: THE Famous Quote

head: "CAG is a ..."
Meaning
rows: prosecutor with a law that hobbles his functioning

law does not clearly indicate the audits he is to perform; does not give adequate powers to obtain documents from government; audit queries are not answered properly, yet law gives no power to act against departmental officials who refuse; so the law itself makes him shaky

can clearly indicate a case of financial fraud but cannot punish; can only make allegations in the report to Parliament; action stays at the government's discretion; can establish guilt but not pass punishment
after his report goes to Parliament and then the PAC, he has no power to question or appeal on action taken; if Parliament and government pay no heed to his report he has no power to challenge it

body: Effectiveness of an audit depends on (1) system for evaluating CAG reports: by Parliament and PAC: adequate discussion time, members present. In the USA and UK the CAG is part of the legislative branch; in India independent of both legislature and executive; a long-pending reform is to make CAG part of the legislature so Parliament debates reports more seriously, holding government accountable and improving financial governance.

(2) Quality of audit reports: under INTOSAI guidelines senior auditors from other countries review India's audit process and make recommendations (and Indian auditors go abroad): the peer review mechanism. First peer review of India's CAG in 2012 found around 50% of CAG's irregularity allegations were not backed by concrete evidence.
